Defamatory Posts on Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn and X: How to Get Them Removed

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

Defamatory posts on Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn or X can be removed in Italy, but the order of steps matters. First preserve the evidence, then use the platform's legal or Digital Services Act reporting form rather than the ordinary report button, and keep a criminal complaint or a court order in reserve for authors and platforms that do not cooperate.

Can you remove defamatory posts from social media?

Yes, when the post contains false statements of fact or gratuitous insults that damage your reputation, and when you report it through the right channel. Social networks act quickly on content that breaks their community rules, and under the Digital Services Act they must also assess notices about illegal content, which in Italy includes defamation under art. 595 of the Criminal Code.

The obstacle is rarely the law; it is the process. Most people press the standard report button, choose a generic reason such as harassment, and receive an automated reply saying the post does not violate the rules. Defamation on social media is a legal question that moderation teams handle in a separate flow, with separate forms, and a notice sent there must be precise enough for a reviewer to decide without knowing you.

Preserve the evidence before anything else

Collect evidence before reporting, contacting the author or replying publicly. Once the author realises a complaint is coming, posts are often edited or deleted, and comments disappear with them. A removed post that you cannot prove existed is of no use to a lawyer or to the Polizia Postale.

  1. Copy the direct URL of the post and of the author's profile; note the numeric profile ID where visible, because display names can be changed.
  2. Take full screenshots showing the text, author, date, number of reactions and shares, and the comments that repeat or amplify the accusation.
  3. Save the page as a PDF or web archive file, and record the date and time of each capture.
  4. For serious cases, obtain a certified copy: a notarial report or a forensic acquisition with a hash value, which Italian courts treat as far more reliable than screenshots.
  5. Keep a log of every report you file, with reference numbers and the platform's replies.

Shares and reposts deserve the same care. On Facebook and LinkedIn in particular, a post shared into groups can reach audiences the original author never addressed, and each copy may need its own report.

Reporting flows on Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn and X

Every major platform offers two routes: the in-app report for community-standards violations, and a separate legal or DSA form for content you consider illegal. Defamation belongs in the second route, while insults, threats or fake profiles may also be handled through the first.

PlatformIn-app report suitsRoute for defamation
Facebook and InstagramBullying, harassment, hate, impersonationMeta's form for reporting content that is illegal under local law, including defamation
LinkedInHarassment, fake profiles, misinformationLinkedIn's illegal content and legal removal request forms
XAbuse, private information, impersonationX's form for reporting illegal content in the EU

Facebook and Instagram

Meta handles both services through the same legal team, so one well-prepared notice format works for both. Posts in private groups and comments are covered as well, provided you can supply the exact link; for private groups this often means asking a member to share it with you.

LinkedIn and X

On LinkedIn, defamation usually concerns professional reputation: accusations against a former employer, a competitor or a business partner. The platform is sensitive to false claims about named professionals, and impersonation reports are effective against fake company pages. X moves faster but publishes less detail on its decisions, so keep copies of every notice you send.

Writing a DSA notice that gets results

A notice under art. 16 of the Digital Services Act must allow the platform to identify the content and understand why it is illegal without a legal investigation. Vague complaints are rejected; specific ones are acted upon.

An effective notice includes:

  • the exact URL of each post or comment, never just the profile;
  • the precise words you consider defamatory, quoted in the original language with a short English translation;
  • why they are false, with documents where possible, such as a judgment, a contract or a registry extract;
  • the legal basis, namely art. 595 c.p. and, for posts published to a wide audience, the aggravated form for offences committed through any means of publicity;
  • your name, email and the statement of good faith that the form requires.

The platform must give you a reasoned decision. If it refuses, you can use its internal complaint system, then an out-of-court dispute settlement body certified under the DSA. In Italy the Digital Services Coordinator is AGCOM, which supervises how platforms apply these rules. Our article on platform liability after the Digital Services Act explains these duties in more detail.

Legal options in Italy when reporting is not enough

If the platform refuses and the post causes real harm, the criminal and civil courts can order removal. Italian case law treats a defamatory post on a public profile or in a large group as aggravated defamation, because social networks reach an indeterminate number of people.

A criminal complaint (querela) must generally be filed within three months of learning of the post, with the Carabinieri, the police or online through the Polizia Postale portal. The prosecutor can request the preventive seizure of the content, which platforms comply with by blocking it, and can ask the platform to identify an anonymous or fake account. Creating a fake profile in someone else's name may also constitute impersonation (sostituzione di persona) under art. 494 c.p. On the civil side, an urgent application under art. 700 c.p.c. can obtain a removal order quickly, while an ordinary claim seeks damages from the author.

Evidence first, legal notice second, court third. Reversing the order is the most common reason defamatory posts stay online.

Comments, shares and public replies

Removing the original post does not remove the copies. Screenshots of the post, quote shares on X and comments under other people's content all need to be tracked and, where they repeat the accusation, reported in the same way.

Whether to reply publicly depends on the audience. A calm, factual reply can help when customers or colleagues have already seen the post, but it also adds visibility and should never contain threats. When a post has gone viral, the response becomes a crisis matter, as shown in our case study on recovery after a viral post; for videos, the approach in our guide to negative video content applies. To remove slander online you need to treat each copy as its own case.
